On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, the Master ascended the hall and raised up his bowl, asking Wáng Suíxiàng, "Since it could not be lifted at the head of Dàyù Peak, why is it now in the hands of this humble ruler? Later, the venerable teacher Címíng said:
"Your Majesty possesses great strength. The assembly, tell me: is there strength in the wrist? Is there strength in ruling the world?
Try to judge for yourselves. Entering the hall, he said: "The Venerable Zhaozhou said: 'One who acts as a patriarch must engage people with matters of fundamental division.'"
The *Lotus Sūtra* may be said to have gained its name in vain. Why? Whenever a Chan practitioner arrives here, we cannot help but engage them in some verbal entanglement;
yet it is nothing more than coarse gruel and plain rice—there is not a single point that constitutes the fundamental matter.
At another time, on a later day, he will see Old Man Yama. How can he clear his name?

Is there anyone among the assembly today who possesses great compassion and can clear his name for the sake of the *Lotus Sūtra*? Is there such a person? Is there? After a long silence, he said: "Familiar faces fill the world;
how many can truly know one's heart?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function operate simultaneously.
To understand the meaning within this, it is like striking the third watch at noon. He then let out a shout and asked: "Where is the guest? Where is the host?
What do you call 'illumination'? What do you call 'function'? He shouted three times in succession.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said, "If there is even a single hair’s breadth [of duality], you call it a single hair’s breadth.
The ancients have already struck it away for all of you. Now tell me, what kind of matter has been accomplished?
He struck the meditation seat once with the staff.

Ascending the hall, when the assembly had taken their places, he took up his staff, drew a line across it, and said, "The pattern has already been revealed. But tell me, how can one avoid falling into error?
He continued, "As it is said: 'Use a wedge to extract a wedge. He struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Dharma Flower loves to show off his donkey’s muzzle; he simply wants to reach the bottom at every step.
Although a patch-robed monk does not understand, it is like salt falling into vinegar."
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: Once Xuansha mistakenly took some medicine, and his entire body became red and festering.
A monk asked him, "What is the solid, unchanging Dharma-body? Xuansha replied, "Drips of pus. Later, Master Huai composed a verse on it:
"Drops and drips—his whole body is festering pus; On the fishing boat, he reveals his family style. People of this age see only the fishing line, But do not see the reeds [of the marsh]."
"Flowers facing the red smartweed. There was once someone who asked Fahu (Dharmarakṣa) about the Dharma: "What is the pure Dharma-body?
He simply answered him, "The stench of excrement perfumes the heavens. He also said, "A child is born by transformation upon a lotus leaf.
Now tell me, is this the same as the ancients, or is it different? Fahu also had a verse: "The stench of excrement perfuming the heavens is merely coincidental; how could Fahu compare [to others]?"
For Your Majesty’s proclamation: If there were a celestial orifice within the nose, one could travel crosswise at will without needing to pierce through it.
Entering the hall, he said: "Going, going—yet truly not going; on the road, act with goodness. Coming, coming—yet truly not coming;
on the path, do not fall into peril. When the ancients spoke thus, Fahua was not like that: "When going, I go with inspiration; when returning..."
Riding on the momentum of this inspiration, I turn back to converse with you once more.

His nostrils droop down over his large head. He ascends the hall and says: "Awakening to the Way through sound; clarifying the mind through form. He then extends his hands and asks, "Is there? Is there?

Then he shakes his hands and says, "There is not. There is not. He then says: "Having already traversed the great ocean, one need not boast of its waves; having left behind Mount Wu, one need not praise its clouds."
[Zhaozhou] always struck the meditation seat with his staff.
Entering the hall, he said: "This matter is like being at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff; one must know how to let go of their hands and feet."
He then struck [the floor] all the way to the bottom. Yet, he could not let go of his life-force.
Today, Fahua, without moving even a single hair’s breadth, teaches everyone to go all the way to the bottom. He then cast down his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ancients said, 'The more one speaks, the further one strays from the Way. But this is not so for the Lotus Sūtra. Even if words fill the world, why is this?
For in navigating a boat, there is naturally a person who holds the helm."
Ascending the hall, he raised the teaching of the Middle Way: "Do not give rise to the mind through form; do not give rise to the mind through sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas.
"Great assembly," he said, "the Old Śākyamuni has here cast his entire body down and out.
He further said, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. What recourse is there? If you cannot save him, you become even more unfilial children.
To eat his rice for nothing—here you must step forward. But tell me, how do you step forward?
(He struck the meditation seat once.
He then ascended the hall and cited Master Yunmen: One day, as Yunmen opened the door, he saw a monk coming. Yunmen then asked him: "Great..."
"When the Great Function is manifest and no rules are observed, what then? The monk had no reply. Yunmen said, "Ask me.
The monk then asked, "When the Great Function is manifest and no rules are observed, what then? Yunmen shook both his hands and called out loudly, "Śākyamuni Buddha is coming!
"The assembly! Old man Yunmen is truly capable of swinging his arms while walking."
It illuminates the past and soars through the present. But what can one do about the eyes of bystanders? Tell me, what kind of eyes do these bystanders possess? He then said:
"If you wish to exhaust the view for a thousand li, you must ascend yet another story."
He arrived at the place of the Fourth Patriarch, Master Nan-ch'uan, and requested him to ascend the seat. He then said: "At Mount Lu, we walked hand-in-hand;
there was nowhere that anyone knew of. Now, in the plains of Huai, you accompany me once more in my lofty steps, yet you wish to emerge before others.
O Great Assembly, when we were at Mount Lu, why was it so profound and secret? And now today, why is it so manifest and revealed? He did not speak further.
The Path of Seeing. To sell gold, one must encounter a buyer for gold.

Upon arriving at the Fifth Patriarch’s [monastery], he ascended the seat and said: "In years past I rested here briefly; today I pass by once more. The sun and moon flow like a stream, and nearly two years have passed.
Now tell me, is there a principle that is without obstruction? O worthy ones, enjoy this lofty banquet atop White Lotus Peak."
[The Master] said, "Below [the mountain]. "I am an old man of illness, dwelling deep within Mount Fahu (Lotus Mountain).

It is but a day’s journey away. How do you explain the principle of being 'without obstruction'? Is it not thus: 'Night after night one sleeps embracing the Buddha; morning after morning one rises together with him.
Rising and sitting, we always follow one another, like a shadow following a body'? If you say this, you are speaking of the second head; you have not yet spoken."
He wears the crown of right concentration. But tell me, how would you say it? He then said: "The vast expanse of the universe—people do not recognize it;
as before, his nostrils hang down with their great heads."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In studying the Way, one must first learn poverty; once you have learned poverty, the Way will become intimate.
When one day you realize the Way of being poor, the functioning of the Way will be like that of a poor person. Although Fahua walks the same path as the ancients,"
Furthermore, I do not follow the same path as the ancients when returning home. Why is this so? I dwell in a small courtyard of my own;
when guests arrive, there is nothing to provide for them, nor anything for them to chew upon. Fortunately, those below me provide support, allowing me to get by each day with mere coverings.
As it is said: "The mountain flowers do not neglect the power of cultivation; the spring breeze naturally takes care of them."
Ascending the hall, he said: "From the beginning at Deer Park until the end at the Bahudhika River, throughout forty-nine years, I have never spoken a single word.
But tell me, what did I say? Then he said: "The peony blooms upon the face of the Bodhisattva;
the palmyra leaves scatter over the head of the yakṣa."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The day of the winter solstice marks the birth of the first yang; from antiquity to the present it has been thus.
All know how to receive blessings in accordance with the season; hereafter, do not fall asleep."
The donor offered his Dharma robe. The Master ascended the hall and said: "A dragon wears but a single thread; even the Golden-Winged Bird cannot swallow it.
Had he swallowed it all at once then and there, would not all under heaven have been at peace? But tell me, which is that which cannot be swallowed?
He then picked up a corner of the robe and showed it to the assembly, saying: "Is this not that which cannot be swallowed? Do you see it? Liang...
Jiuyun said: "Casually draped over one's shoulder, it is still superior to the people of this age wearing brocade robes.
He ascended the hall and raised the following case: A monk asked Nanquan, "The mani-jewel no one recognizes; it is intimately held within the Tathāgatagarbha."
"What is the treasury? Nanquan said, "That which comes and goes with you is the treasury. The monk asked, "What about when there is no coming or going?
Nanquan said, "That too is the treasury. The monk then asked, "What is the pearl?
Nanquan called the monk's name. The monk responded. Nanquan said, "You do not understand my words. "Great assembly, this monk possessed one *maṇi* jewel."
The "Niche Pearl" may truly be called a treasure rare in this world. How deeply pitiable its existence!

It nearly fell into a ten-thousand-fathom abyss, yet it relied on the old man Nanquan, who personally reached out his hand to lift it up for it. But tell me, where does this pearl reside now? He then said:
"The Sea God knows its preciousness but not its price; he has left it for the human world to shine through the night."
Record of the Sayings at Qianming Chan Monastery on Longmen Mountain in Shu Prefecture, compiled by the junior disciple for study, Zhihua.

On the day the Master accepted the invitation, he ascended the hall. A monk asked: "The Dragon Gate has extended an invitation for the Master to attend in person; what is the matter for the Dharma Flower today?"
"How is it? the Master said. "When the tally arrives, it is executed. The monk said, "If that is so, then where the Elephant King walks, all solitary tracks cease.
The Master said, "For now, you should set your mind at ease. The monk said, "I shall see you off after the midday meal. The Master said, "Thirty years from now. The monk bowed. The Master then said:
"The picking up of the flower and the entrustment at Vulture Peak were spoken in vain; to receive it personally, one must manifest many bodies while seated. The Dragon... [text ends]

At the entrance there is a separate aperture. Upon reaching this point, the transmission of the teacher is not established; yet it is transmitted from generation to generation, universally responding to all levels so that the ancestral style does not fall.
Great assembly, since the transmission of the teacher is not established, why is it nevertheless transmitted from generation to generation?
After a long silence, he said: "The leaves fall one by one as autumn deepens; the blossoms open petal by petal as spring warms.
The next day, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Longmen? The Master said, "Only those who arrive know it. "What is the person within the realm?
The Master said, "Both feet planted firmly on the ground. The monk said, "I have received the Master’s instruction regarding the person and the realm. As for..."
"What is the matter regarding the supreme vehicle? The Master said, "Who knows the distant mist and waves? There is another way of thinking.
The monk said, "In that case, in the morning I watch the clouds drifting slowly; in the evening I listen to the water murmuring. The Master said, "Prostrate yourself! Then he said:

"When seeing and hearing are not yet shed, they are like the moon in the water. Every day there are mountain colors and the sound of water, famous flowers and extraordinary birds, filling [the senses]."
The eyes are full; the ears are deaf. How can one explain the principle of liberation? Do you wish to understand? It is flowing, it is flowing!
Old Śākyamuni has no skillful means. Enough, enough! The scenery of Longmen Mountain and Water is the most secluded in the world.
Last night I slept until dawn; where there is elegance, let there be elegance.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Dharma has no differentiated dharmas; it is through delusion that one clings to them. The entire earth is clinging;
the eighty-four thousand pores are all nothing but clinging. But tell me, where does one cling? After a long silence, he said: "Clouds atop the ridge peaks never find rest;
water flowing down the ravine is too vast and wild."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is it like when one has not yet passed through the Dragon Gate? The Master said, "This is not the right tune.
The monk asked, "What is it like after passing through? The Master said, "This is not the right tune. The monk hesitated, and the Master said, "The transaction was not settled."
He then said: "To seek the ox, one must inquire after its tracks; to study the Way, one must inquire after the mindless. When the tracks are found, the ox returns;
when there is no mind, the Way is easy to find. He raised his staff and said, "The tracks are here; where is the ox? He then struck the ground once with the staff.
Ascending the hall, he said: "All sounds are the Buddha’s voice; all forms are the Buddha’s form.
Old Śākyamuni has deceived the men and women of this world, casting them into the Avīci Great Hell, where they remain to this day without being cleared of their guilt.
Raising his staff, he said: "The butcher Xiang Dabo from Taihu County—today, at Longmen, upon my staff..."
"Upon his head, he attained perfect enlightenment, turned the Great Dharma Wheel, and delivered all sentient beings. Do you people see this?
If you do, then all under heaven is at peace. [He struck the meditation seat with his staff and descended from the seat.]
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "The Tripitaka Master with Large Ears searched for the National Teacher three times and could not find his body.
I wonder where the National Teacher was? Zhaozhou said, "He is inside the Tripitaka Master's nostrils.
The monk asked Xuansha, "If he is inside the nostrils, why can't he see him? Xuansha said, "It is precisely because he is too close. "Great assembly," [the Master said].

If the National Teacher were inside the nostrils of the Tripitaka Master, what would be difficult to see? Little do you realize that the National Teacher is actually inside the eyes of the Tripitaka Master.
He ascended the hall and said: "When Baizhang first visited Mazu, he saw wild ducks; because of this, he received a blow on the bridge of his nose."
Suddenly there was a point of entry. Later, he went to consult [the Master] again. Under a single shout, his ears were deaf for three days; only then was it exhausted. Now tell me:
how far apart are the place of total severance and the moment under the shout? After a long silence, he said: "Have you not heard it said:
'In heaven and on earth, there is only I'? Then he let out a shout.
Ascending the hall, he said: "When one engages in such contemplation, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear. But tell me, how does one contemplate?
If you contemplate with a mind of grasping, then the entire earth is a forest of thorns. If you contemplate with a mind of non-grasping, then the entire earth is a wilderness of barren peaks.
After a long silence, he said: "Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Those who study Chan and seek the Way must not be muddled. If you can penetrate through to the Dharma-body, the Northern Dipper is hidden away.

I am now old and decrepit, too weary and indolent; when meeting people, I lack the strength to engage in discussion. Only the hoe knows my Way: it plants pine trees while walking together up to Vajra Peak.
Old Master Dongshan Cong may truly be said to have gathered his profound mechanism before its signs appeared, concealing his dark workings.
In this very transformation, the elegance of their style is difficult to match across the ages. This old man by the Dragon Gate is struck daily by chronic indigestion;
day by day he grows weaker, becoming increasingly emaciated and truly lacking in strength. Even so, when discussing matters with others, he still says:
"Though it be thus, poverty at home is better than having a neighbor who is poor."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Sometimes the tip of the pestle blossoms; sometimes the Buddha’s face has a hundred flaws.
When Lord Li falls drunk on the street, it is simply because Lord Zhang is drinking wine. The lantern wrinkles its brow in distress; the pillar laughs aloud and claps its hands."
Ascending the hall, he said: "For those who have not yet penetrated through, let them first recognize it; for those who have already penetrated through, you must walk together with them.
The entire earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa—whom would you have recognize it? On the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust is received;
toward what place, then, could one walk? Therefore it is said: 'Where others dwell, I do not dwell; where others walk, I do not walk.'"
It is not that it is difficult for people to gather together; rather, it is mostly because the distinction between the monastic and the lay must be clearly defined.

One might think to subtract a little from where there is little and add a little to where there is much. Why, then, subtract further from what is already little and add further to what is already much? This is a secret of the immortals, not transmitted even between father and son.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today it is this very thing; tomorrow it is also this very thing. What is that thing?
You lacquer buckets—go to the meditation hall!"

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: A monk asked Dongshan, “When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? Dongshan said, “After the fire has burned out, there is a single stalk of thatch. Longmen, however, is not like this. When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? He replied: [The Master continued: “If you can see it here, you will understand the meaning of the ancient’s words. But if you do not see it, you must look further.

Do not merely say, ‘He has gone to the Western Paradise,’ for that is not the ultimate destination. Nor should you say, ‘He has returned to his original source,’ for that too is a provisional expression. So, where exactly does he go? If you can discern this, you will see that the ancient’s words were not in vain. If you cannot, you must reflect upon them deeply. This is why the ancients said: ‘The path of words is cut off; the mind-ground is empty. Only when you have reached this state can you truly comprehend the meaning of the ancient’s words.”
"The walls have ears. Ascending the hall [to teach], he said:
"I am not afraid that thoughts arise; I only fear that awakening is late. What words were these of the ancients?
The entire great earth is Śākyamuni; where else could there be sentient beings? The entire great earth is sentient beings; where else could there be...
Śākyamuni, although it is thus, tell me: where does the Dragon Gate let its body fall?
If there is anyone who knows, I shall divide half the monastery with them to dwell together; if not, seek it within the alms bowl.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
Even if it were to manifest before him, he still would not have attained the Way of Buddhahood. Why is this so?
If you wish to avoid incurring karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata."
Preface to the *Zutang jiangji* (Outline of the Patriarchal Hall) from the *Baoyun yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Baoyun), Volume One:
Our Way flourished in this land, beginning with the patriarch Bodhidharma as its guiding principle; he was the one who first established the Zen monasteries.
The *Zhì* (Regulations) are the chronicle of Baizhang Dazhi; this is indeed what the world universally knows.

Yet, how is it that within the ancestral halls (*zutáng*) of the world, each takes the successive patriarchs of their own founding mountain as their ancestors? This is truly a failure to reflect upon one’s own lineage and progenitors.
Is this not the most supreme of all that has been transmitted and upheld? Alas! Five hundred years after the Teaching arrived, Bodhidharma first came.
Did the worthy masters of the various schools of the past not know that nature itself is the Sage? Why did they ultimately remain mired in the mud of regarding nature as the Sage?
It was only necessary for a mere snap of the fingers after the Shaolin era for [the truth] to be expressed without relying on words.
Silently transcending existence and non-existence, one is suddenly liberated from all dependencies and spontaneously returns to the fundamental source.

Furthermore, those of antiquity who dwelt in caves and lived in rock shelters took only the Dharma as their excellence and its flavor; they did not at all consider that those dwelling within it might become arrogant.
Only the Great Wisdom Chan Master (Dazhi Chanshi) foresaw this, and he resolved it through the regulations of the Chan forest. It was by relying on these that Shaolin [flourished].

This tradition remains vibrant throughout the world to this day. I desire that within the ancestral halls of the world, Bodhidharma, the Great Wise One, be placed in his correct position, with those who successively transmitted the founding of the mountain [the patriarchs] accompanying him.
This is to honor the arrival of later generations by respecting their origin and returning to the source of greatness—is this not so?
Established on the first day of the tenth month in the third year of the Xīníng era, the cyclical year Gēngxū.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Baiyun Yuan, Volume Two:
The Record of the Xinghua Chan Monastery in Shu Prefecture,
Compiled by the Disciple-Student Chu Ning.
On the day the Master opened the hall, after the incense had been offered for the Emperor and the mallet had struck, he said:

"If you were to disperse just like this, the ancestral flame would have shone forth in its full glory. But since that is not yet the case, we must level the high and descend to the low. Therefore it is said:
'The Way of our Great Sage does not reside in speech, nor does it reside in silence; it is not concerned with speech, nor is it concerned with silence. It is simply this..."
This one person shines brilliantly alone, far transcending past and present. Abiding within the space between past and present, he acts in accordance with the moment.
Is there anyone today who knows the timing? He brings forth this matter and meets with Xinghua. A monk asked: "The imperial canopy has personally arrived at this Dharma assembly;
we pray that the Master will proclaim the secret meaning of the West. The Master said: "In the midst of the Five-Peak Song, he beats the Dharma drum. This one person.
"Few people know the news within. The monk said, "In that case, the pure breeze pervades the earth. The Master said, "One cannot hear it.
The monk said, "Thirty years from now, someone will raise this story. The Master said, "Excellent. The monk bowed. Another monk asked:
If one attains sudden enlightenment through a single word, what benefit does it bring to the person? If one does not attain enlightenment through a single word, what loss does it cause the person?
Looking up, there are no Buddhas; looking down, there are no sentient beings. How do you speak that single phrase for turning the body? The Master said:

"Who knows that beneath this straw hat is originally the same person who was once full of sorrow? The monk said: "In that case, neither sages nor ordinary people can grasp it; even Yao and Shun would not know it."
[The monk] said, “Master. The Master said, “You know only one; you do not know two. The monk said, “I thank the Master for providing proof.
The Master said, “Do not mistake the calibration of the scale. The monk responded with a nod. The Master said, “Thirty years from now, you must look into this for yourself. The monk bowed.
The Master then said, “When Great Master Bodhidharma first came to this land, no one yet understood him.”
At Shaolin Temple, he sat upright and composed in meditation for nine years. One day, the Second Patriarch stood in the snow with it reaching his waist.
Bodhidharma asked, "From where have you come? The Second Patriarch said, "I ask the Master to pacify my mind. Bodhidharma said, "Bring me that mind."
"I shall settle your mind for you. The Second Patriarch remained silent for a long while and then replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unattainable.
Bodhidharma said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. The assembly, tell me: where exactly was it that Bodhidharma settled the Second Patriarch's mind?
If one says that when seeking the mind it is ultimately unattainable, such that not a single dharma can be grasped by the intellect—this is the place where others find peace of mind.
But as for this very message of speaking in such a manner, from what source does it come? If one says that which speaks in such a manner...
This is the place where others find peace of mind. Yet they do not see the Way; they take the "mind" to be a great affliction and the "principle" to be a great obstruction.

If one directly grasps the mind and principle and sweeps them both away until nothing remains, suddenly and expansively, this is one's own native land. A mountain monk has a verse that says: From beginning to end, seeking the mind, it cannot be found.
Vast and empty, no person of Shaolin is seen. The old snow fills the courtyard; once again its cold is known. The nostrils remain as they were before, tucked back in place.
The upper lip. At this very moment, the heavens and earth, the entire great world, are all a single gate of liberation.
Śākyamuni has no room here to set hand or foot; the entire Tripitaka of teachings serves merely as a footnote.
Thereafter, shifting his body and changing his step, responding to things and meeting the occasion, he is able to flow forth the entire Tripitaka of teachings. Therefore it is said: "Skillful..."
"Every word spoken is that which words cannot express; every step taken is that which steps cannot trace. This is to let go;

yet, "the myriad plants are eternally in spring"—this is to hold fast. Thus, though the great earth may be free of dust, even so, it does not yet accord with the style of a patch-robed monk (*śramaṇera*).
But tell me, what is the style of a patch-robed monk? After a long silence, he said: "The momentum of a thousand peaks reaches the mountain peak."
"Resting at the edge; ten thousand streams of sound return to vanish upon the sea.
He ascended the hall and said: "When the autumn river is clear and shallow, the white heron blends with the misty isle.
How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! His entire body lies amidst the wild grasses. Great assembly, today Xinghua has a precedent to follow."
Ascending the hall on the first day of the New Year, a monk asked: "I do not ask about 'the early spring is still cold'; what is the realm of Xinghua? The Master said:
"Every household looks upon the night child. The monk said: "White clouds constantly unfold by the banks of the Xiao and Xiang rivers;
the entire assembly in the hall receives your grace. The Master said: "You have no share. The monk bowed. The Master then said: "The years go by, the years come back."
In the comings and goings, how many ways are there of welcoming the new and seeing off the old? On the street, one bumps into Uncle Zhang;
the beginning of the New Year’s reign is quite senseless. Still muttering that the early spring is cold, the sound of the bugle on the city wall rises as one piece;
everyone joins in celebrating the joy of ten thousand years.

The Successor (Yunmen Wenyan) offered tea and ascended the hall, saying: "Cāṇakya picking up the flower and transmitting it to Kāśyapa is adding mud upon earth; severing an arm to find peace of mind is grasping at the moon in water.

Tell me, how was this lineage obtained so that it has not fallen into decline until today? After a long silence, he said: *Note: This passage describes the transmission of the Dharma from Śākyamuni to Mahākāśyapa via the gesture of holding up a flower, and the subsequent lineage of Chan masters. The green mountains do not lock in the power of its long flight; the vast blue sea surely knows the height from which it comes.
Entering the hall, he said: "Even dharmas should be relinquished, let alone non-dharmas. Picking up his staff, he said: "This staff—"
Furthermore, how does one relinquish it? And how does one speak of that which is not the Dharma? After a long silence, he said:
"Knocking off the nostrils, exposing the eyes. He struck the meditation seat once.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you do not clarify a single dharma, it will cloud your eyes. Picking up his staff, he said: "Is this not the eye?
Within the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, there is not a single trace; within the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates..."
"Every gate is liberation. How can you obstruct him? Even as you see mountains and waters every day, and distinguish blue, yellow, red, and white—this is not him;
how then do you see him? He then struck his staff once and said, "Blind!"
He invited the Librarian to ascend the hall. [The Master] cited the case of a monk who sat cross-legged for long periods inside the Sutra Hall.
One day, the Librarian asked him, "Why do you not read the sutras? The monk replied, "I do not know how to read. The Librarian said, "Why do you not ask someone else?"
The monk bowed deeply with palms joined and asked, "I do not know what character this is. The Librarian remained silent.
"Great assembly, although the Librarian was speechless, how could his voice not have been like thunder? Although this monk did not recognize the character, its strokes were nonetheless distinct.
Tell me, what character is it? After a long silence, he said, "Go seek it within the *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon)."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "Before one's parents were born, where was the nose?

The Master said, "The flowers must bloom through the night; do not wait for the morning breeze. The monk said, "I have come specifically to seek your instruction. The Master said, "Your eyes have been changed.
The monk said, "If that is so, then you, Master, have a point of excellence. The Master said, "Have you received a beating yet? The monk bowed.
The Master then said: "The ancients said: 'When a thief comes, you must strike; when a guest comes, you must look upon them. This is the constant way of propriety.
But when it comes to 'striking when a thief comes,' tell me, how does one strike? A human face resembles that of a thief; a thief’s face resembles that of a human. At the third watch of the night..."
"What room for discernment is there? Nevertheless, even so, one must not let it pass. With this, he struck once with his staff and ascended the hall, saying:
"I have always told you that [the matter] is not yet complete; I have no other intention. It is simply that you all must eat your congee and rice.
You must pick up the spoon and set down the chopsticks yourself before you can be full. If you rely on someone else to prepare it for you, then..."
This is a hollow fullness. On the thirtieth day of the tenth month, one gains nothing but a single bout of dry swallowing of saliva.
Nevertheless, do not let it be forgotten by the mouth.

On the day the Master opened the hall, after the proclamations had been read and the mallet struck, he looked out over the assembly and said:
"Before the drum has even sounded, and before this mountain monk has yet ascended the seat—what a fine model of an ancient Buddha! If anyone can realize it at this moment..."
It is attained. One might say that Śākyamuni of old was not ahead, and Maitreya of today is not behind.

Yet, even waiting for what is brought forth from the three inches of the tongue, it is already already discordant. There must be a hand capable of sweeping away this discordance before one can rescue it in its entirety.
Is there anyone present today? Come forward and see! A monk asked: "When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, he saved people."
[The Master] finished. "Since you, the Abbot, have opened the hall for the Dharma six times, how many people have you brought across?

The Master said: "When walking, one reaches the end of the water; sitting, one watches the clouds arise. The monk said: "If that is so, then ten thousand years to the Emperor! The Master said: "Everyone wishes for this.

The monk responded with an "Amen" and prostrated. A monk asked: "The imperial canopy overlooks the assembly at this Dharma gathering; we pray that the Master will not withhold the thunderous roar [of the Dharma]."
Yin asked, "The Master says: 'A single lute plays an ancient tune; those from a hundred *li* away celebrate the new sound. The monk said, 'A single phrase has gone far beyond.
The Master said, 'How do you hear it? The monk said, 'My acquaintances fill the world.
The Master smiled at him. Then he said: "One who is skilled in speaking speaks that which cannot be spoken; one who is skilled in leaving traces leaves traces that cannot be traced. Every...
Throughout the day, opening one’s mouth and moving one’s tongue, there is nothing that is not speech. How can one speak of that which cannot be spoken?
Since it is called "speech," it is already a trace. How can one speak of that which cannot be traced? Arriving at this point—
The entire great treasury of the teachings finds not a single word applicable here; yet, having arrived at this point, the entire great treasury of the teachings finds every single word applicable.
Why is it that at first it is not applicable, while later it is indeed applicable? Tell me, where does the confusion lie?
The Way is not seen. The momentum of a thousand peaks ceases at the foot of the mountain; the sound of ten thousand streams vanishes upon reaching the sea.

From antiquity to the present, those who have drilled into and gazed up toward this state are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds; yet those who have truly and thoroughly penetrated it are not even one or two in a hundred or a thousand.
If you can indeed penetrate through, then throughout the twelve hours of the day, you will experience unimpeded joy and respond to circumstances with ease.

All things exist for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings. From the heavens and earth, the stars, the sun, and the moon, down to all the grasses, trees, and forests across the entire world—everything is but a single instrument for entering and exiting, for play. Therefore, the ancients said: "The jade turns and the pearl revolves;
though one masters the words of the Patriarchs and Buddhas, it still defiles the field of the mind. Old Lu only knows how to husk rice; how could he have attained the Yellow Plum?"
A tradition passed down through ten thousand ages. When this mountain monk was in his hermitage, he also instructed his disciples, saying:

"Though there is indeed nothing of the sort directly before you, it is still difficult to remain alive if one has not fully penetrated it. Last night, a wild wind arose at the gateway of the sea; infinite waves were swept away in an instant.
Having spoken thus, he first cleared the great road for others, and then held both hands out before them. There it is!
Those who are sharp and perceptive need not exert even a hair’s breadth of effort to grasp it; can anyone do so today?

If you say it cannot be grasped, I dare ask you all: throughout the twelve periods of the day, when you are engaged in practical activities and discerning between the worthy and the foolish, what is it that you rely upon?
"This is right, that is wrong. What is this?
He ascended the hall and said: "As for the two words 'Buddha-dharma,' to cast them away to another world-system would not be considered excessive. Yet, twice a day the alms bowl must be moistened;
it cannot lack even a single drop. Have you not heard it said: 'When one is constantly satiated, one forgets a hundred hungers'? Now..."
The mountain monk’s own body is this very thing. He then said, "I hope you are well, I hope you are well.

When Official Gu entered the mountains, the Master ascended the hall and said: "Last night upon my pillow, I composed a verse on the mountain to express my gratitude to the great scholar Gongfu, an old friend from twenty years ago at Mount Lu.
Today he has traveled so far to visit Baiyun with such diligence; it truly ought to be..."
I present this to the great assembly. After having requested [the teaching], I shall clearly present it to those in all quarters. Does this verse merely thank the great scholar Gongfu? No;
it is intended to strip away the fleshly sweat-soaked shirt from every monk in the world who possesses nostrils.
Do not say I have not spoken. It says: "The Great Man above, Qiu Yiji; he transformed three thousand seventy scholars. You, little students, eight..."
[The Master] said, "Jiuzi (Nine Sons) was a man of refined virtue who could understand the rites.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "At the winter solstice, the first yang arises. Thereupon, the Master raised his sitting cloth and said, "Tell me, what is this?
The Master struck the meditation seat once. The monk said, "What can one do about it being blown by the wind and scorched by the sun? The Master said, "Answer."
"Can you even speak of it? The monk clapped his hands twice. The Master said, "You have only attained half a wedge. The monk said, "I thought it was truly so.
The Master said, "It is still somewhat lacking. The monk bowed. The Master then said, "Today is the festival of the first yang."
Speaking thus, tell me: is this merely the circulation of worldly conventions, or does it have another point of reference?
If you can discern this here, then after the birth of the first yang, throughout the four seasons and eight nodes, the myriad phenomena will share the same light as all people.
"Is there anyone who can divide this up? Today Baiyun cannot help but divide it for you. He then said: "The movement of the sun's shadow shifts; the winter solstice arrives.
May you receive blessings in accordance with the season; may all be auspicious and appropriate."
When Elder Zhongfeng arrived, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the red leaves parting from their branches;
how is it to perform the play upon meeting the occasion? The Master said, "A holeless flute blown on both sides.
The monk said, "If so, then everywhere there is song and chant, celebrating peace. The Master said, "Who is the one who knows this? The monk said, "Ra-ra-li ra-ra-li."
The Master said, "You are still halfway there. The monk said, "Master, please take note of this clearly. The Master said, "That will do. The monk bowed. The Master then said:
"Nine times nine is eighty-one; how many people can calculate that? Two five-hundred coins."
Originally, it is all one. When you arrive at this point, can even a single coin be added?

If there were something that could be added, then light would surely shine along the entire path, transcending past and present. Yet, from antiquity to today, thousands upon tens of thousands have only loved to follow the lead of others.
Today, Baiyun shall add for you. He then said, "Descend from the seat and hand over the duties to the administrative officers and the head monk."
The assembly was seated. Inviting Master Zhongfeng to ascend the seat for the first time, he entered the hall.
A monk asked, "The thousand sages do not seek it; they loathe their own selves. For whom do you communicate the message of coming and going?
The Master said, "We travel the same path, yet our strides differ. The monk said, "How can one evade the eyes of the multitude? The Master said, "One foot is in front, and one is behind."
The monk stepped back. The Master said, "If it were not for the flowing water intervening, you would surely have crossed over to another mountain.
The monk said, "It strikes the very crown of my head. The Master said, "Monk, you must not forget this. He struck him, and the monk bowed.
The Master then said, "With a single invocation of 'Namo Buddha,' all have already attained the Way of the Buddhas. He snapped his fingers once and said, "Now tell me, how many are there?"
"Too few! Is it not that one is all, and all is one? If you understand it in such a way, how can there be any clarity?
Tell me, then, what is it? He then said: "Everyone they meet says they have retired from office; yet among those beneath the forest trees, not a single person has ever been seen.
He struck the meditation seat once.

Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "When Vimalakīrti remained silent, he was walking his own private path; how does the Master propagate the Dharma? The Master said, "Going east, one does not see the benefit of going west. The monk said, "In that case, there is emerging and submerging. The Master said, "Where is it? The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "It is still right here. The monk said, "Do not say that you do not meet anyone. The Master said: [The Master continued: "If you do not meet anyone, who is it that speaks these words? If you can point out this person, then you may have some understanding of the Way. But if you cannot, then you are merely following after words and chasing shadows. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "If you do not understand, then go and ask the old man on the mountain peak. The monk said, "What is the meaning of 'the old man on the mountain peak'? The Master said, "He has been sitting there for a long time; why do you not ask him? The monk bowed. The Master said, "Bowing is easy, but what about when you meet him face-to-face? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "You have met him, yet you do not know him. The monk said, "How can I know him? The Master said, "If you do not know him, how can you avoid being deluded by appearances? The monk said, "Delusion and awakening are both empty. The Master said, "Empty of what? The monk said, "Empty of all dharmas. The Master said, "If all dharmas are empty, then who is it that says they are empty? The monk was at a loss. The Master said, "This is why it is said that even if you attain the Way, you must not forget the source; if you forget the source, you will lose the Way. The monk said, "What is the source? The Master said, "The source is the very place where you are now asking questions. The monk said, "How can I recognize it? The Master said, "If you try to recognize it, you are already lost. The monk said, "Then how can I find it? The Master said, "Finding it is like finding a lost horse in the middle of the night—it is not something you can grasp with your hands. The monk said, "Is there no way to reach it? The Master said, "Reaching it is like reaching the bottom of the ocean—you cannot fathom its depth. The monk said, "Then is there no way to realize it? The Master said, "Realizing it is like realizing a dream within a dream—it is not something you can awaken from. The monk said, "If so, then what is the ultimate reality? The Master said, "The ultimate reality is that there is nothing to be attained, nothing to be realized, and nothing to be spoken of. It is simply this: the ordinary mind is the Way. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master said, "If you can understand this, then you will know that the Buddhas of the three times and the patriarchs of the ten directions have all emerged from this very place. If you cannot understand it, then you are merely wandering in the dark, lost in the dust of the world. The monk said, "I am grateful for your instruction. The Master said, "Instruction is easy, but what about when you encounter a situation? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "Silence is good, but what about when you encounter a person? The monk said, "Encountering a person is like encountering a mirror—there is nothing that is not reflected. The Master said, "A mirror reflects forms, but what about when you encounter the One who is beyond form? The monk said, "Beyond form is the Great Void. The Master said, "The Great Void is vast and boundless, yet it is not something that can be grasped. If you can grasp it, then you have already fallen into a trap. The monk said, "Then how can I avoid falling into a trap? The Master said, "Avoiding traps is like avoiding the net of Indra—it is not something you can escape by running away. The monk said, "Then how can I enter the net? The Master said, "Entering the net is like entering the net of Indra—it is not something you can do with effort. The monk said, "If so, then what is the ultimate liberation? The Master said, "Ultimate liberation is like the liberation of a bird in flight—it leaves no trace behind. The monk said, "If there is no trace, then how can there be any teaching? The Master said, "Teaching is like the echo of a valley—it responds without premeditation. The monk said, "If so, then I have attained some understanding. The Master said, "Attaining understanding is easy, but what about when you encounter a crisis? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "Silence is good, but what about when you encounter a question? The monk said, "Encountering a question is like encountering a sword—there is nothing that can withstand it. The Master said, "A sword cuts through things, but what about when you encounter the One who is beyond cutting? The monk said, "Beyond cutting is the Great Emptiness. The Master said, "Great Emptiness is profound and mysterious, yet it is not something that can be conceptualized. If you can conceptualize it, then you have already fallen into a pitfall. The monk said, "Then how can I avoid falling into a pitfall? The Master said, "Avoiding pitfalls is like avoiding the pit of Māra—it is not something you can do by seeking outside yourself. The monk said, "If so, then I have finally understood. The Master said, "Understanding is easy, but what about when you encounter the ultimate truth? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "Silence is good, but what about when you encounter the living spirit? The monk said, "Encountering the living spirit is like encountering the wind—it moves everything without obstruction. The Master said, "The wind moves things, but what about when you encounter the One who is beyond movement? The monk said, "Beyond movement is the Great Stillness. The Master said, "Great Stillness is tranquil and serene, yet it is not something that can be dwelled in. If you dwell in it, then you have already become stagnant. The monk said, "Then how can I remain free? The Master said, "Remaining free is like remaining in the midst of a great fire—it is not something you can achieve by extinguishing the flames. The monk said, "If so, then I have truly realized the Way. The Master said, "Realizing the Way is easy, but what about when you encounter the ultimate mystery? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "Silence is good, but what about when you encounter the ultimate reality? The monk said, "Encountering the ultimate reality is like encountering the ocean—it is vast and deep, yet it is not something that can be measured. The Master said, "The ocean is vast and deep, but what about when you encounter the One who is beyond depth? The monk said, "Beyond depth is the Great Equality. The Master said, "Great Equality is impartial and universal, yet it is not something that can be grasped. If you grasp it, then you have already fallen into a duality. The monk said, "Then how can I avoid falling into duality? The Master said, "Avoiding duality is like avoiding the net of the fisherman—it is not something you can do by casting the line. The monk said, "If so, then I have finally reached the end of the road. The Master said, "Reaching the end of the road is easy, but what about when you encounter the ultimate destination? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "Silence is good, but what about when you encounter the ultimate realization? The monk said, "Encountering the ultimate realization is like encountering the sun—it illuminates everything without exception. The Master said, "The sun illuminates everything, but what about when you encounter the One who is beyond illumination? The monk said, "Beyond illumination is the Great Darkness. The Master said, "Great Darkness is obscure and hidden, yet it is not something that can be entered. If you enter it, then you have already lost your way. The monk said, "Then how can I find my way back? The Master said, "Finding your way back is like finding your way back from a dream—it is not something you can do by waking up. The monk said, "If so, then I have truly understood the essence of the Way. The Master said, "Understanding the essence of the Way is easy, but what about when you encounter the ultimate truth? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "Silence is good, but what about when you encounter the ultimate reality? The monk said, "Encountering the ultimate reality is like encountering the sky—it is vast and open, yet it is not something that can be grasped. The Master said, "The sky is vast and open, but what about when you encounter the One who is beyond openness? The monk said, "Beyond openness is the Great Emptiness. The Master said, "Great Emptiness is profound and boundless, yet it is not something that can be conceptualized. If you can conceptualize it, then you have already fallen into a trap. The monk said,
"You must examine this more closely. The Master then said: "Regarding this matter, there is one person who can carry it;
its value is equal to the three thousandfold world-system. There is another person who cannot carry it; it is not worth half a coin. Now tell me:
what is the three thousandfold world-system? And what is that which is not worth half a coin? He then said: "Have you not heard it said: 'Only by knowing gratitude does one [attain]...'"

To explain the repayment of gratitude, he ascended the hall and said: "Raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye; brandishing a mallet, holding up a whisk; snapping fingers, clearing the throat—all these are but snares and traps.
Tell me, will those at Haihui Temple escape this today or not? He then said: "Every household has Avalokiteśvara."
While at Mount Mìtí (Wutai), the Master ascended the hall and said:
"The end of summer and the beginning of autumn are inconceivable; take a step and move your body—you may know it for yourself.
The four seas all sing of the transformation of Yao and Shun; yet how can they compare to the *ra la li* beyond the clouds?"

Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Master Dongshan Wuben, who said: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, you must go where there are ten thousand miles of ground with not a single inch of grass.
A monk cited this to Layman Liuyang. The Layman said: "As soon as one steps out the door, it is already grass. The Master said:
"If you can see the Layman, you will see the old man Dongshan; if you see the old man Dongshan..."
Thus one can see that Master Dongshan was easy to perceive, while the Hermitage Master was difficult to perceive.
This is because he was not bound by the constraints of being an abbot. As it is said: "The clouds atop the ridge peak never rest; the water flowing down the ravine is too busy."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Not valuing one's own spirit, one seeks liberation; for whom do you communicate the news of coming and going? The Master said: "I do not know. The monk said:
"Once a word has been uttered, even four horses cannot overtake it. The Master said: "How would you divide it? The monk said: "The bystander laughs. The Master said:
"Indeed, you have not yet divided it. The monk said: "I am accustomed to passing before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, my hand..."
Holding the golden bells, he celebrates the Great Peace. The Master says, "Tut, tut! The monk bows. The Master then says:
"The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action (*wuwei*). This is the field for selecting Buddhas; with an empty mind, one returns having passed the examination.

In the daily activities and applications of life, people speak of all manner of things—yellow and white. If you call this "mind," then there will be no time of passing the examination. If you do not call it...
Even if one sets one's mind to it, there will never be a time of passing the imperial examination. But tell me, how does one attain the "passing of the examination with an empty heart"?
After a long silence, he said: "I told you he was a dragon, yet you would not believe; as expected, he has indeed won the embroidered banner."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "The great earth is covered in vast snow; wherever we meet, everyone says it is cold. Why is it that one cannot pass beyond this?
The Master said, "Look with your own eyes. The monk said, "If so, then not a single flake falls elsewhere."
The Master said, "And you say it cannot be passed over. The monk said, "I thought the red-bearded one was the only one; there is yet another red-bearded barbarian.
The Master said, "So that is who it is after all. The monk bowed. The Master then said, "Master Shitou asked Master Rang:"
"To not seek the liberation of the sages, while not honoring one's own numinous spirit—how can this be? Letting asked, "Your question is too high;
why not ask something lower? Shitou said, "I would rather sink into the abyss for eternal kalpas than seek the liberation of the sages."
Xuedou took up the case and said, "Whom shall I have eat thirty blows? The Master said, "Everyone, who knows that the old man Xuedou has left behind this staff?
Today it is given to Baiyun. Since this is so, I also wish for everyone to know.
He struck the ground once with the staff.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Baizhang said, 'You all shall cultivate the fields for me, and I shall preach the Great Meaning for you.

When the monks had finished cultivating the fields, they came forward and said, 'The field cultivation is complete; we pray that the Master will preach the Great Meaning. Baizhang walked several steps."
He stepped back and stood, extending both hands. The Master said, "The Great Assembly: Baizhang’s exposition of the Great Meaning ends here.
As for those who were present at that time and went on to further study under Mazu—where have they gone?
If you say there is more to it, you will inevitably be like painting legs on a snake. Now tell me, how do you perceive the place where the old man Baizhang stands? He then said:
When guests arrive, there is no tea or refreshments; mugwort broth serves as the ritual offering.
Entering the hall, he said: "If you can truly achieve a single outpouring of sweat, then even upon a single blade of grass, the jade towers and crystal palaces will manifest.
If you have not yet achieved a single outpouring of sweat, then even if jade towers and crystal palaces exist, they are but..."
It is covered over by a single blade of grass. Tell me, how can one get out through the sweat? After a long silence, he said:
"I have a pair of hands for the destitute; I have never easily performed the *Santai* dance."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an old case: A monk asked Master Beichen, "What was the meaning behind Jia Shan’s beating of the kitchen steward?
Xian immediately struck him. As the monk hesitated, Xian instead asked the monk, "Do you understand?
The monk said, "I do not understand. Xian said, "How much salt and vinegar have I wasted for you! The Master said: "Tell me, did Beichen see the ancients? If you say he acted toward the staff..."
"Looking down at Jia Shan is much like swinging a staff to strike at the moon. If you do not see it in this way, tell me:
in whose hand does the staff lie? He then struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To take up one and let go of another has been so from ancient times until now. But tell me, what is the phrase for taking up one and letting go of another?
He then said: "The green forest secretly changes its leaves; red buds continue to open their flowers."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Master Xinghua once said to the monk Kebin, 'Before long, you shall become a master who leads the assembly.
Kebin replied, 'I will not enter your community. Xinghua asked, 'Do you refuse to enter because you have already understood?'"
[He] would not comply and did not enter. Kebin said, "In no way will I do so. Xinghua then struck him and said, "Gentlemen, the rector Kebin has been defeated in the battle of Dharma.

He shall be fined five strings of cash and provide a full meal for the assembly. On the following day at the time of the midday meal, he further removed his bedding and expelled him from the monastery.
Later, when Kebin went out into the world to establish a monastery, he instead offered incense to Xinghua. [This is recorded in the] Conglin...
From antiquity to the present, everyone has said that Kebin was the *vinaya* master who knew gratitude and thus understood how to repay it.
To speak in such a way is to bury the ancients; it is like adding mud upon dirt. But tell me, how do you see Kebin the *vinaya* master?
Do you wish to understand? Although he burned incense for Xinghua, he nevertheless sought to perfume the heavens and scorch the earth himself. Furthermore...
Listen to this verse: "Clearly and brightly, the place of heat is for this person; if one acts as this person, one will sink beneath the waves.
One must see where Master Bin grasped it up; its fragrance pervades heaven and scorches earth even unto this day."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Its merit exceeds that of the two polarities, yet it lacks benevolence; its brilliance surpasses that of the sun and moon, yet it is ever more obscured.
Master Zhaor only attained half. But tell me, what is the complete state? He then said: "The left eye is half a catty;
the right eye is eight taels."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Master Māda said, 'This very mind is Buddha,' and he also said, 'Neither mind nor Buddha.
Do you all wish to see Master Māda right now? Everywhere the green willows can tether the horse; at every household’s gate, one passes through to Chang’an."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Sometimes opening one's mouth, one cannot express it; sometimes opening one's mouth, one can express it.
Between being able to express it and not being able to express it, what difference does it make? A majestic qilin has but a single horn."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A snap of the fingers, a cough; a raising of the eyebrows, a twinkling of the eyes—none of these are not this very thing.

Why, then, did the ancients say: 'The moon in the empty expanse over the ten-thousand-year-old azure pool; only after repeated stirring can one finally know it'? Do you wish to understand? If you wish to understand?"
"Eighty-one. He ascended the hall and said:
"For those whose ground is secure and firm, the style of the ancient Buddhas remains. For those who sport with supernatural powers, the present Buddha manifests his radiance.
But tell me, is this now the ancient or the present? Then he said: "When mounting a horse, one sees the road; when reaching the post, one displays the majesty."
It was accomplished.
He ascended the hall and said: "When the ancients left behind a single word or half a phrase, as long as it had not been penetrated, it was like bumping into an iron wall.
Suddenly, one day, after seeing through it completely, one finally realizes that the iron wall was oneself all along. Now tell me, what about now?"
"How do you penetrate this? He then said, "An iron wall, an iron wall.

Ascending the hall, he said: "If one can utter a single phrase completely, one acts as a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If one cannot utter a single phrase completely, one acts as a teacher to gods and men.
Today, how will you speak? He then said: "Where there is water, it contains the moon; where there is no mountain, it does not bear [the moon]."
Yun ascended the hall. A monk asked, "You and I are alike; we have no affinity. Tell me, today do we have an affinity or not?
The Master said, "When meeting, one does not drink wine; even the mountain flowers laugh at such a person. The monk said, "If that is so, then acquaintances fill..."
"In all under heaven, how many people truly know the mind? The Master asked, "As for the matter of knowing the mind, how would you say it?
The monk replied, "If one is not an enemy, one does not meet. The Master said, "You are still somewhat off the mark. The monk bowed.

The Master then said, "Now that you have arrived here, can you avoid the criticism that says, 'Raising a child is a matter of karmic affinity'? "Can you avoid it? Can you not avoid it? He continued, "It is chillingly solemn."
The style is pure and refined. Yet, poor Sudhana; he has failed Maitreya.
He ascended the hall and said: "One, two, three, four, five—there is too much left over. Six, seven, eight, nine, ten—and yet there is a little too little.
Now tell me, how can one weigh it exactly upon the pivot of the scale? Then he said:
"In the end, the frosty night moon falls naturally into the stream before me.
He ascended the hall and said: "Though the conditioned is false, to abandon it is to fail in the path of practice. Though the unconditioned is true, to cling to it is to obscure the nature of wisdom.
If the ancients had taken this as a path to travel upon, the entire earth would have been contained within it."
"Under the heels. "If you head toward the city of Chang'an, you will lose an entire boatload of people.
"Do you all wish to see Baiyun’s sickly old self? He then said: "Holding the flute once to play the tune of returning home, I blow it deep into the night past the Mulu Bay."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Clearly and vividly known—this is simply this very thing. Why, then, do you fail to penetrate it?
It is only because when you see someone open their mouth, you immediately call it 'words and phrases'; and when you see someone close their mouth, you immediately call it 'a long silence.
Furthermore, it is said that in movement, action, speaking, and breathing, throughout the entirety of the ten directions of the world, there is nothing that is not it."
This is why it is said: "While on the road, he remains obscure, still harboring old resentments.
Have you not seen how Master Yunmen said, "Hearing sound, one awakens to the Way; seeing form, one clarifies the mind"? He then raised his hand and said, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva!
Here, take this coin and buy some fried cakes. Lowering his hand, he said, "It turns out, however, that they are steamed buns. Furthermore—

I see it. When I was at Fahua, I once addressed the assembly, saying: "Master Wuye said, 'If even a single hair's worth of thoughts regarding holy or ordinary beings is not exhausted, one will inevitably enter the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse.

O Great Assembly, even if you were to suddenly exhaust every last thought regarding holy or ordinary beings down to a single hair, you would still inevitably enter the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse. You blind fools!"
"Just look like this.

[The Master] ascends the hall while the plaque bearing the name of the monastery is being hung. A monk asks: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sovereign attains the One and governs the world.
What can a patch-robed monk do by attaining the One? The Master says: "The sprout is severed at its root from the ground. The monk [remains silent].
The monk said, "If that is so, then when cold comes one turns toward the fire, and when hungry one eats. The Master said, "Eighty thousand miles. The monk said, "It is so.
The Master said, "The assembly sees you. The monk bowed. The Master then said: "The Dragon-Comfort Sea-Assembly has news unheard before;
The golden plaque hangs high, shining upon the white clouds. One enters the pavilions and towers with a mere snap of the fingers— Between the eyebrows and the eyelashes."
One must distinguish them. The eyebrows and eyelashes have their long and short; even if you say they are neither long nor short, you have not yet escaped the view of permanence.
To further say they are long-long and short-short is like adding frost to snow. Tell me, how is it so? He then said: "Distinguish them."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: Guishan asked Yangshan, "Where have you come from? Yangshan replied, "From the fields.
Guishan asked, "How many people are there in the fields? Yangshan stuck his hoe into the ground and stood with his hands clasped behind his back.
Guishan said, "Today on South Mountain there are many people mowing thatch. Yangshan pulled out his hoe and walked away. The Master said, "Yangshan’s response was like this..."
Correct. The count is indeed clear; it is simply that you have driven the spade too deep.
Guishan merely wanted two five-hundred coins to equal one thousand; he was not delighted by obtaining a donkey. Why is this so?
"When the family prospers, filial sons are born; when the state is hegemonic, there are strategic ministers."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When opening one's mouth, the very last word is precisely what hits the mark.
When taking a step, the very last step is precisely what treads upon it. Why, then, is the nostril ultimately not straight? It is simply because we usually see him as stubborn;
therefore, we are unwilling to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment. Today, Baiyun exhorts you all to arouse it! He then said: 'One.'"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Originally a guest upon a fishing boat, I happened to shave my beard and hair and don the *kāṣāya*.
I cannot remain within the ranks of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; last night, as before, I slept among the reeds. As before, I sleep among the reeds—who is there with whom to share?"
The bright moon fills the boat; there is nowhere to ask. Sandpipers occasionally call out two or three times.
Entering the hall, he said: "Yunmen cited Jiaoshan’s words: 'As soon as a single speck of dust arises, the entire earth is fully contained.
Nanquan [Niaokuo] picked up a tuft of cloth-hair, and immediately someone was awakened. Everyone, where is Yunmen not right? Nevertheless..."
"One must pass straight through the nostrils. He struck his staff once and ascended the hall, saying:
"If you can directly perceive with clarity and take it up, yet someone says 'this is not it,' you will immediately see a discrepancy.
Otherwise, you will recklessly take things up; otherwise, you will lose what was before and forget what follows. Tell me, where does the sickness lie? It is simply this."
Because there is no time yet when one has attained penetration, this very thing is not it. All celestial mechanisms have been exhausted, yet there is not a single point of leakage.
After a long silence, he said: "Not it, not it."
Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Yunmen, who said: "All day long I eat rice, yet I have never bitten into a single grain.
Why is it that all day long he eats rice, yet has never bitten into a single grain? If you say he bites into them, you contradict Yunmen;
not only do you contradict Yunmen, but where would you yourself go? If you say he does not bite into them...
[The Master] said: "How can you achieve satiety within? Do you wish to understand? With the three virtues and six flavors, offer to the Buddhas and the Sangha;
let all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm universally partake in this offering."

Ascending the hall, he said: "If there is even the slightest inclination toward attainment, one will ultimately find no place of return. If one can truly face this, day by day one withdraws from activity until all worldly interests are exhausted.
Suddenly, one beholds one’s own original father and mother. But how is it that they are the original father and mother?
He then said: "Ten thousand blessings! Ten thousand blessings!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Every phenomenon is from the beginning the Dharma; there is no phenomenon and no non-phenomenon.

Why, within a single phenomenon, would there be both phenomenon and non-phenomenon? Great assembly, those who wear the *kāṣāya* are monks; those who wear crowns are Daoists; those who wear caps are scholars.
Yet it is also said that they are neither monk nor layperson, and possess neither the marks of male nor female. So, how is this?"
After a long silence, he said: "A single breath remains silent, yet contains all forms; where can the myriad spirits offer thanks for this impartiality?

Ascending the hall, he raised the case of the lay practitioner Gan Zhi, who constantly received guests. Whenever a monk asked him, "Receiving guests is no easy task," the practitioner would reply: "It is not difficult."
The attendant said, "It is like feeding a donkey or a horse. Master Jue of Langye said, "Quickly bring the rice!
"The assembly, Langye has hands that do not commit offenses. Even so, Baiyun does not think so.
It is like feeding a donkey or a horse; I wish that the attendant would remain forever as he is today."
Ascending the hall, he said: "All obstacles are ultimate awakening. Śākyamuni Buddha was not clever;
he has been rendered useless, his nostrils pierced by the staff of Baiyun. Tell me, can this be forgiven?
He then said: "Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī; liberation is liberation. He struck the floor with his staff once.
He ascended the hall and said: "When all the worldly arts have been mastered through practice, they naturally develop a surplus of grace.
But tell me: when the arts of a patch-robed monk have been mastered through practice, how much surplus grace is there?
After a long pause, he blew a single blast on his horn and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "As soon as something is raised, there is the intimate and the remote. Tell me, which one is the intimate? Which one is the remote?
After a long silence, he said: "Dangerous!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; his manifestations number in the hundreds, thousands, and tens of billions. He then struck the meditation staff three times and said:
"From time to time he reveals himself to those of this age, yet those of this age themselves do not recognize him. Having struck the staff, he descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "In the Great Peace, one cannot remain still; until old age, one dwells amidst the white clouds.
The most expedient place is right before one’s gate, where there is a fine mountain. To stroll there casually once surpasses the ingestion of the Great Elixir of Reversion.
Why does it surpass the ingestion of the Great Elixir? He then let out two sighs."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of National Teacher Longya, who said: "All famous mountains were reached because of my feet;
through many years of toil, they have been worn down like socks. Now that I am old and can no longer walk, I hold in my hand a broken wooden ladle.
The Master remarked, "The old man Longya may truly be said to find it difficult to forget what he is most familiar with."
Ascending the hall, he raised this case: A monk asked Yangqi, “What is the Immovable Honored One? Yangqi said, “The assembly must all exert their strength together.
Baoyun, however, does not say it so. What is the Immovable Honored One? Prostrate yourself!
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the example of Master Dongshan, who said: "When the sky is clear, cover the house; when the time comes, reap the grain.
Once the tax has been paid to the Imperial Ancestors, one beats the belly and sings songs. "Tell me, Great Assembly: how does the Chan elder Dongshan Cong compare to the elder Baiyun?"
Official Yang of Huangmei invited [the Master] to ascend the hall. A monk asked, "The blazing clouds have just rolled away and the jade dew has first descended;
the worthy magistrate is present at this assembly—please, Master, preach the Dharma. The Master said, "The pine and cypress are only high when they are only humble.
The monk said, "If one proceeds in this very manner, what then? The Master said, "When you see that green, what do you see? The monk said, "After many years, one sees the heart of man. The Master...
The Master said, "Speak more carefully. The monk said, "I beg the Master to speak instead. The Master said, "A Chan guest such as you is still only halfway there.
He then continued: "From antiquity to the present, those who discourse on principle and phenomena are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds;
those who understand Chan are even more so. Yet all are merely seeking a person of their own household, like selecting the moon from among the stars in the sky."
It is as if so. The worthy magistrate of Huangmei, Yang Cigong, has heard my name for over ten years. Last night, he suddenly paid me a visit;

it turns out he is truly one of our own people of the house. Though I have not yet counted every single item—whether the length of the ladle's handle or the size of the cauldron—their number is nonetheless quite clear. It may be said that he is as if already here in the East.
Xixi said: "When flowers bloom and leaves fall, how many times have I intended to cast gold to forge a Zichqi?
Yesterday, when Gongfu of Dangtu came, he recited 'Shang Daren' once. Today, Cigong has come; you must recite it once more.
At nightfall, while sitting coolly in the hall, he suddenly heard someone calling out: "Official Yang of Huangmei has arrived at Baiyun!"
Pàn: "I have long heard that you have secretly stolen from my school, yet I have not been able to confront you to settle this.

One night before the lamp, as we passed through old public cases (gong'an), you confessed each offense one by one, wishing for all to see. Your nose is straight and your cheekbones are high; you are truly a man of immeasurable capacity.
On what day will you tread the prosperous thoroughfare? My Way shall then shine brilliantly, and together we shall sing the song of Great Peace, sweeping away all under heaven."

[The Master] was disordered [in his speech]. His literary compositions did not obstruct others; he was also proficient in the *Dayan* (Great Divination) calculations. "Two fives make ten"—as before, they constitute a single thread.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked: "The ninety-day period of *jinzu* (protection of the feet) is now complete; we pray that the Master will distinguish the weight of the wax man. The Master said:
"If even one's own actions are not permissible, who could go on to interfere with others?
The monk said, "In that case, the measure is clear. The Master said, "Everyone they meet says they have retired from office; yet where has anyone ever been seen beneath the forest trees?
The monk said, "Six times six is thirty-six. The Master said, "Say it again. The monk said, "One, two, three. The Master said, "The assembly!"
The proof is as follows: Baiyun has spent another summer there, exhausting all the old stories of Vulture Peak.
Although he shifts from east to west to patch things together, he continues to dominate the discourse to this very day.
Ascending the hall, he said: "I have come to this land to transmit the Dharma and save those whose minds are deluded. Did the Patriarch not know this?
'One flower opens into five petals; the fruiting occurs naturally. It is like using the wind to fan a fire—no great effort is required."
Ascending the hall, he said: "By abstaining from provocative flavors, all ailments naturally diminish; yet with many attachments, one cannot avoid occasional weariness.
Living in poverty, every movement results in either compliance or resistance; thus, one must attain the single flavor of pure leisure.
Nevertheless, do not say that a 'mindless' state is the Way—for even this 'mindlessness' remains separated by a further barrier."
Ascending the hall, he said: "That which all of you see every day, and that which all of you use every day, is as if descending from the heavens or surging up from the earth;
it flows on continuously without the slightest interruption. It can truly be said that the ancient Śākyamuni did not precede it."
Now Maitreya is not late; Baiyun is sick and old. Having failed to meet a true master at the start, he has ended up as nothing but a relic.

He ascended the hall and said: "Perfect realization sinks into the ocean of consciousness. Since it is perfect realization, why does it sink into the ocean of consciousness? Thereupon, he picked up [his whisk].
Holding up his staff, he said: "It is precisely because we call this thing a 'staff' that it is so. Now tell me, how can one return to one's original station?
He then held the staff upright and said: "Staff! Staff!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Caution and entreaty damage your virtue; non-reliance is truly efficacious. Let the blue seas change as they may, I shall never speak for you.
This is yellow clay; which one is white stone?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "From the beginning we have lived together, yet you do not know my name. You blockheads! Let things take their course and just walk along like this.
One foot in front, one foot behind—since ancient times even the most sagely worthies have not recognized this;
is it truly so? How could ordinary, common folk understand it in their haste? It is like adding flowers upon brocade."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: A monk informed Zhaozhou Zen Master, "The Great King is coming to visit you, Master.
Zhaozhou said, "May the Great King enjoy ten thousand blessings. The monk said, "The Great King has not yet arrived. Zhaozhou said, "And yet you say the Great King has come.
The monk was at a loss. The Master said: "Although the monk was at a loss, what could he do? The King's command had already been executed. Once the King's command has been executed, it is so."
"The seas are calm and the rivers clear. But tell me, how do you express this phrase "the seas are calm and the rivers clear"? He then said:
"The rustic old man knows nothing of the labors of Yao and Shun; he beats the drum loudly to sacrifice to the River God."
